meta.title: Why 2026 is the LAST NORMAL Year for Tesla, SpaceX and Humanity
meta.speakers: Jo Bhakdi (host of the stream), James (co-host, 'Coffee with Friends')
meta.thread_line: 6 threads · AGI by field and the last normal year · Tesla-SpaceX merger math · Cybercab and Megapack economics · gigawatts in space · terrestrial compute and Musk's moat · midterms and tech vs politics

snapshot: Part two of a joint livestream (captions are disabled; this brief is built from a local Whisper transcript, so figures and spellings are as heard).
Bhakdi says AI is by-field AGI: it will exceed humans on **more than half** of what humans do by end of next year, and 2026 is the last normal year.

He is more bullish on SpaceX than ever after its earnings call, calls Tesla's call noisy, and models a Tesla-SpaceX merger at a **30%+ premium**, near 3 SpaceX shares per Tesla share within 18 months.
Cybercab is the near-term Tesla driver: about 80,000 paid miles a day growing 10% a week, with 3.3M miles and zero accidents, per the speakers.
First gigawatt of compute in space is called for **2029-2030**; SpaceX is said to plan 2.7 GW of terrestrial compute by end of 2026 and 10 GW more next year.
Musk's edge is framed as supply: cooling, turbine blades, chips and 300,000-GPU coherent clusters, while neoclouds like CoreWeave lose years and billions to delays.
On politics, the speakers say history favors stocks after midterms and that Wall Street likes gridlock; they also see a widening split between tech and the Democrats, framed as 'Snow Crash'.

themes.title: Why this is the 'last normal year': AGI arrives field by field
themes.lead: Bhakdi says AI already exceeds humans in some skills and will exceed them on more than half of human work by the end of next year, so the near-term risks are political and cyber, not sci-fi.
bullets: Radar-chart framing: AGI fills the whole circle of human skill and ASI exceeds it, but today AI is far beyond humans in math (called 'cooked') and coding, and still weak in writing.
He wrote in early 2025 that there would be three years of a 'singularity continuum' from January 2025 to December 2027, and says we are well past halfway; his errors have been on the slow side.

A host notes that AGI-2040 talk, even from leaders like Demis Hassabis two years ago, is now off the table, and that ChatGPT launched four years ago with the next 12-24 months expected to be 'completely insane'.
He puts a loss-of-control ASI scenario deep in the 2030s and says it distracts from near-term issues: political disruption, the shift from labor to capital, and cybersecurity.
Cyber warning: hacks and exposures of key systems (power plants, groceries) arrive daily, so personal security should be locked down.

quote.text: more than half of everything that humans do, AI will exceed humans by end of next year, I'm pretty sure

themes.watch: Both speakers are retail investors in Tesla and SpaceX; Bhakdi also runs a community site and tracker that benefit from attention to this thesis.

themes.title: SpaceX's call was the best he's seen; Tesla's merger math is the new driver
themes.lead: Bhakdi says Elon's remark that committees on both sides are discussing a merger moves Tesla toward a deal with at least a 30% implicit premium.
bullets: Bhakdi calls the SpaceX earnings call the best he has ever seen and is 'more bullish than I ever was on SpaceX'; Tesla calls are 'always a little depressing', with 11 signal nuggets buried in noise.
Pre-call context: Elon was criticized on X by two people right before the Tesla call, and Bhakdi believes it affected his demeanor.
Merger: he sees about **99-100%** odds, within 18 months, and the 'most litigated merger in history', so no tricks and independent committees.
Premium: a Wall Street standard of 30-40%; with Tesla near 350 that implies roughly 493 (30%), 520 (37%), a stock at 500 needing about 650; he sees 500-550 from here.
Exchange ratio: he expects about **three SpaceX shares per Tesla share** if prices stay near today's, and rejects floor theories.
Urgency: the longer they wait, the more a SpaceX run-up (10 GW of extra compute next year) hurts Tesla holders.
A host adds Ron Baron sees SpaceX at $50T in 10 years; Elon reportedly said more than $100T in under 10 years barring a major world war, and half a trillion to a trillion in revenue.
Bhakdi defends the Tesla CFO, who reportedly saved about $5B of capex.

quote.text: I don't believe in the floor theory at all.

themes.watch: Bhakdi says he bought SpaceX a little early and was hurt by yesterday's sell-off; the host also holds the position. Premium and ratio figures are their own estimates.

themes.title: Cybercab unit economics, and a trillion-dollar Megapack business hiding in plain sight
themes.lead: The hosts argue Cybercab miles and Megapack profits are underpriced, and that the cars could double as distributed inference compute.
bullets: Per a host, Tesla's robotaxi does about **80,000** paid miles a day at roughly $2.50 a mile, growing 10% a week, which would reach a million miles by year end; the cars are in Austin first.
The speakers say Tesla has 3.3M miles with zero accidents and, from something read at 5 a.m., may now exceed Waymo's paid miles in Austin.
TAMs: Cybercab around $10T; optimistic around $30T. Gross profit per Cybercab: $15-30K a year, manufacturing cost $15,000, life of about a million miles.
Equivalence debate: one gigawatt of compute is worth roughly 300-500K Cybercabs (Bhakdi) versus a million (host); with about $11B vs $40B yearly profit per gigawatt, depending on depreciation.
Megapack: about 130-140 (GWh) of capacity, around $33B revenue at 33% margin is ~$11B profit; at 100x PE that is $1.1T for a company at $1.5T. A host says this was predicted in a paper years ago.

Distributed compute idea: AI5 chips in millions of Cybercabs, Megapacks and Superchargers (75,000 stalls, empty at night) linked by Starlink could add inference capacity; roughly 1.2M Cybercabs could equal 10 GW of inference.
Inference thesis: CPU demand could rise 10x with agents; the heavy cooling on Cybercab is speculated to be for GPUs.
themes.watch: Many numbers are heard from speech and flagged by the speakers as rough ('I'm totally winging this'); novelty pricing is acknowledged to wear off.

themes.title: The first gigawatt in space by 2029-2030
themes.lead: Bhakdi models SpaceX reaching its first orbital gigawatt in 2029 at best and 2030 conservatively, with launch cadence and pads as the constraints.
bullets: Starship should be ready to deploy by end of next year; Nvidia and SpaceX are building an orbital version of the Vera Rubin 72-rack scheduled for **Q4 2027**, so scaling starts in 2028.
A gigawatt needs roughly 15,000-20,000 tons; SpaceX has asked for about 450 flights a year; Bhakdi's bull case is 24 flights in 2028 and 75 in 2029.
Bottleneck debate: the host stresses reusability (catching booster and Starship on test flight 15) and ramping to six launches a month; Bhakdi expects launch pads to become the limit by 2031-2032.

SpaceX is said to be adding about a gigawatt-scale block every 30 days to reach 2.7 GW this year and 10 GW next year at around $50B a gigawatt of capex; a host models 12.5 GW live by end of next year.
Satellites are expected to be around 240 kW, so about 4,000 per gigawatt with laser links, fine for inference but not for tightly coupled training.
Why space: the 'walls are coming in' on terrestrial compute, with permits and local resistance getting harder each year, so orbit is perfectly timed for 2028-2029.
The permit conundrum: Elon says he has a 'magic hack' he won't share, and the speakers think siting in pro-build states like Louisiana, Tennessee and Texas is part of it.

quote.text: I think they will potentially hit the first gigawatt in space, either 2029, best case, or 2030

themes.title: Why Elon can build compute while neoclouds can't: a supply problem, not demand
themes.lead: Bhakdi says demand is effectively unlimited, so winners are those who can stand up compute fastest, and SpaceX has secured cooling, turbines, chips and 300,000-GPU clusters.
bullets: Elon is reportedly securing about **20 GW** worth of cooling for next year; cooling and wiring are his bottlenecks, and chips, memory and land are already handled.
Turbines: when manufacturers said they couldn't get blades from the only three suppliers, SpaceX started casting blades with rocket-engine casting technology.
A rumor says he locked up 40% of Vera Rubin supply; coherent clusters of 300,000 GPUs versus others' roughly 30,000; data centers built in about 12 weeks and paid back in under 12 months.
Neoclouds: CoreWeave's build time went from 2.5 to 4 years, with each year of delay costing about $5B of interest at 15%; Bhakdi is not invested and sees them as supply-constrained.
Hyperscalers are 'toast' without compute (Google reportedly buying compute from Elon); H100 rental prices on a compute futures market are higher than six years ago.
Revenue scale: half a gigawatt makes a $26B run rate; a host expects a gigawatt to command about $72B by 2030.
Macro view: the AI sell-off ('fake bubble, nubble') is nearly over after maybe one more week; SpaceX and other AI names look undervalued on PEG ratios.

quote.text: It's not a bubble. I call it a nubble.

themes.title: Midterms, gridlock and the tech-versus-Democrats split
themes.lead: The speakers say history favors stocks after midterms, that Wall Street likes a paralyzed DC, and that politics is now a fight over AI and tech power.
bullets: Over 19 midterm cycles since 1950, markets were up about 8% three months after election day, about 14% at six months and 20-32% at twelve; history shows 'a dip and a rip' around uncertainty.
Bhakdi expects the Republicans to hold the Senate and calls blue-red-red (a Democratic House with the Senate and presidency unchanged) the best Wall Street outcome.
He argues Wall Street prefers gridlock because politicians who can act raise debt and taxes, regardless of party.

Tech and politics: Silicon Valley has become a closed front against the Democrats, who attack AI and billionaires; Bhakdi says money managers like BlackRock, Blackstone and Apollo are investing in AI, so torpedoing AI hits them.
He frames the future as 'Snow Crash' (corporations over governments), with Elon's media ownership push seen as a bid for reality control; the hosts say they are analysts, not activists.
Taxes: both see tax regimes tightening globally (unrealized gains, billionaire taxes, crypto monitoring), pushing geographic arbitrage.

quote.text: Wall Street likes when DC is paralyzed.

themes.watch: Strongly partisan commentary from two investors who hold Tesla and SpaceX; the media-ownership and sponsorship remarks are unsourced asides.

takeaways.title: Watch Tesla-SpaceX merger committee news and the implied 30%+ premium before sizing either position.
Track Cybercab weekly paid miles and the Austin-versus-Waymo comparison as the near-term driver.
Follow Starship flight 15, reusability and launch cadence against the 2029-2030 first-gigawatt call.
Test any neocloud against build time and interest cost, not demand.
Treat the midterm sell-off as a historical dip, and check the exposure to gridlock outcomes.
Lock down personal security accounts, since AI is accelerating cyber risk.
